title: The Lord's Day
hook: every Sunday is a little Easter

segments.voice: Yesterday, Saturday for Mary, the day of waiting before the morning. Your line was saturday is hers. Did you give it a quiet minute? Day six hundred ninety-three.

Say the word for Sunday in Spanish: domingo. In Italian: domenica. In French: dimanche. In Portuguese, domingo again. Every one of them is a worn-down form of the same old Latin phrase, dies Dominica, the Lord's day. English kept the sun. But half of Europe, every single week, quietly says what the day was for. Christians didn't pick it at random. They picked it because of one particular morning, very early, outside a tomb.

All four Gospels agree on the timing: the women came to the tomb early on the first day of the week, and it was empty. So the first day became the Christians' day. In Acts, Paul's community at Troas gathers on the first day of the week to break bread. And the last book of the Bible gives the day its name. John, exiled on Patmos, writes in the Douay-Rheims: "I was in the spirit on the Lord's day." Around the year 150, Justin Martyr wrote to the Roman emperor describing what Christians did on Sunday: they gathered from town and country, heard the writings of the apostles and prophets, prayed, and shared bread and wine, and a collection went to widows and orphans. Read it today and it sounds like Mass. That's why Catholics call every Sunday a little Easter. It isn't a reminder of Easter. It's the same feast, coming round every seven days. The Second Vatican Council called Sunday the original feast day, the foundation of the whole year. The early writers had a lovely name for it too: the eighth day. Creation took seven days; the resurrection is the first day of a new creation, a day outside the old count. Catholics keep it in two ways. They go to Mass, which the Church asks of them as an obligation. And they rest, setting aside work that gets in the way of worship, joy and family. Pope John Paul the Second wrote a whole letter on it in 1998, Dies Domini, the day of the Lord. And this ends week ninety-nine: the Lateran, Christ the King, the months with their themes, then Friday, the Ember days, Mary's Saturday, and now Sunday: the cross, the waiting, the morning.
screen: `THE FIRST DAY OF THE WEEK.` · `I WAS IN THE SPIRIT ON THE LORD'S DAY.` · `JUSTIN'S SUNDAY, AROUND 150.` · `THE EIGHTH DAY: A NEW CREATION.` · then, large: `A LITTLE EASTER, EVERY SEVEN DAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: plan one piece of real rest for this Sunday. Settle, and breathe. Picture next Sunday from morning to night. Where's the noise, the errands, the inbox? Choose one thing to set down for that day: a chore that can wait, a screen, a worry you'll pick up on Monday. Then choose one thing to put in its place: a long meal, a walk, a call to someone you love, Mass if you go. Hold that picture for the rest of the sit. The bell holds the time.
The Lord's Day. Sunday, the first day of the week, when Christ rose; the name comes from the Book of Revelation, and it lives on in domingo and domenica. Today's word.
Your line: a little easter. This Sunday, when you wake, say it once before you check your phone, and keep the one thing you planned. Day six hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics are asked to attend Mass every Sunday (or on Saturday evening) and to keep the day free of work that hinders worship, rest and time with family; many families also keep a shared Sunday meal.
